items.title: Q1 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:
[T]he aim of all solitude...is the same: to live more at leisure and at one's ease. But people do not always look for the right
way. Often they think they have left business, and they have only changed it. There is scarcely less trouble in governing a
family than in governing an entire state: whatever the mind is wrapped up in it, it is all wrapped up in it, and domestic
occupations are no less importunate for being less important. Furthermore, by getting rid of the court and the marketplace
we do not get rid of the principal worries of our life....Ambition, avarice, irresolution, fear and lust do not leave us when
we change our country....They often follow us even into the cloisters and schools of philosophy. Neither deserts, nor rocky
caves, nor hair shirts, nor fastings will free us of them.
                                                              --  Michel de Montaigne, "Of solitude"
Which of the following best captures the theme of the passage?
options: The court and the marketplace must be got rid of
Try what one may, no one can ever be at ease
Ruling a state is easier than managing a family
Solitude is one condition of peace with one self
items.explanation: In his essay 'Of Solitude' (Essais, Book I, Chapter 39), Michel de Montaigne argues that genuine solitude is not mere physical withdrawal from court or marketplace, but achieving inner peace and self-sufficiency within one's own mind.

The mistake human beings make is to:
options: abstain from the love of leisure
items.explanation: Montaigne observes that human beings mistakenly believe changing their physical surroundings brings ease, while they fail to restrain the mind itself, which carries ambition, avarice, fear, and lust wherever it goes.

items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism

                                                              --  Michel de Montaigne, "Of solitude"

The "principal worries of our life" follow us if we:

A. detach our self from family life.
B. are deep into buying and selling.

C. mentally abstain from hustle and bustle.
D. are in to schools of philosophy.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Montaigne explicitly states that 'the principal worries of our life' persist both in the commercial marketplace of buying and selling (B) and even when we retreat into cloisters and 'schools of philosophy' (D).

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem:
Read the following poem and answer the questions that follow:

A Prayer for Old Age
God guard me from those thoughts men think
In the mind alone;
He that sings a lasting song
Thinks in a marrow-bone;

From all that makes a wise old man
That can be praised of all;
O what am I that I should not seem
For the song's sake a fool?

I pray--for fashion's word is out
And prayer comes round again --
That I may seem, though I die old,
A foolish, passionate man.
                                                            - W.B.Yeats

Thoughts true for all time are:
items.explanation: In W.B. Yeats's poem 'A Prayer for Old Age' (1934), the lines 'He that sings a lasting song / Thinks in a marrow-bone' mean that enduring poetic truths are felt viscerally deep inside the self rather than in abstract intellect alone.

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats

Read the following poem and answer the questions that follow:

Thinks in a marrow-bone;

From all that makes a wise old man

For the song's sake a fool?

I pray--for fashion's word is out
And prayer comes round again --

                                                            - W.B.Yeats

In the second stanza the poet thinks of:
options: what all makes a wise old man
what all earns all others' praise
what he does not want to appear
what he thinks he is, a fool
items.explanation: In the second stanza ('From all that makes a wise old man / That can be praised of all'), Yeats prays to be guarded against what he does not want to appear—namely, a conventional, respectable 'wise old man.'

items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats

Which one of the following best captures what we infer about the poet?
options: He believes in the efficacy of prayer
He is an old man wise as old are
He is old but happy in not being wise
He is a foolish young man who thinks wisely
items.explanation: Throughout 'A Prayer for Old Age,' the aging Yeats rejects cold intellectual respectability and rejoices in remaining 'A foolish, passionate man' devoted to poetic intensity.

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:
The earth was made for Dombey and Son to trade in, and the sun and moon were made to give them light. Rivers and
seas were formed to float their ships; rainbows gave them promise of fair weather; winds blew for or against their
enterprises; stars and planets circled in their orbits, to preserve inviolate a system of which they were the centre.
Common abbreviations took new meanings in his eyes, and had sole reference to them: A. D. had no concern with
anno Domini, but stood for anno Dombey-and Son.
                                 - Charles Dickens, Dombey and Son

The whole description is an example of:
items.explanation: This famous passage from Chapter 1 of Charles Dickens's Dombey and Son (1848) uses biting sarcasm and ironic hyperbole to satirize Mr. Paul Dombey's mercantile arrogance in viewing the entire universe as existing solely for his firm.

items.title: Q8 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:
The earth was made for Dombey and Son to trade in, and the sun and moon were made to give them light. Rivers and
seas were formed to float their ships; rainbows gave them promise of fair weather; winds blew for or against their
enterprises; stars and planets circled in their orbits, to preserve inviolate a system of which they were the centre.

Common abbreviations took new meanings in his eyes, and had sole reference to them: A. D. had no concern with
anno Domini, but stood for anno Dombey-and Son.
                                 - Charles Dickens, Dombey and Son

What is the 'system' of which Dombey and Son were the centre?
items.explanation: In Mr. Dombey's egoistic worldview, the solar and natural workings of the cosmos revolve solely to preserve his family shipping enterprise, 'Dombey and Son,' as the center of existence.

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:

Is man no more than this? Consider him well. Thou ow'st the worm no silk, the beast no hide, the sheep no wool, the
cat no perfume. --- Ha! here's three on's are sophisticated. Thou art the thing itself; unaccommodated man is no more
than such a poor, bare, forked animal as thou art.
                                                            - Shakespeare, King Lear
'Is man no more than this?' means:
options: Man is far more than what he seems to be
Man is not as well endowed as some other animals
As an animal, man is a superior animal
items.explanation: In Act 3, Scene 4 of Shakespeare's King Lear, Lear looks at the half-naked Edgar ('Poor Tom') on the stormy heath and realizes that natural, 'unaccommodated man' is a frail, bare creature less naturally endowed with protective coverings than animals.

items.title: Q10 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow:
Is man no more than this? Consider him well. Thou ow'st the worm no silk, the beast no hide, the sheep no wool, the
cat no perfume. --- Ha! here's three on's are sophisticated. Thou art the thing itself; unaccommodated man is no more
than such a poor, bare, forked animal as thou art.
                                                            - Shakespeare, King Lear
Which one of the following best captures what Shakespeare means?
options: Man just uses what animals possess
Animals unlike man are more complex
items.explanation: By declaring 'Thou ow'st the worm no silk, the beast no hide, the sheep no wool, the cat no perfume,' Lear recognizes that civilized humans merely borrow and use external coverings that naturally belong to animals.

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Plato
items.stem: Who among the following was of the view that poetry was only an imitation of an imitation and therefore trivial?
items.explanation: In Book X of the Republic, Plato argues that because the physical world is already an imperfect copy of ideal Forms, artistic mimesis is merely 'an imitation of an imitation,' thrice removed from truth.

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Johnson
items.stem:
In "The Life of Cowley" which two of the following criticisms were made by Samuel Johnson against  a group of writers
he termed the 'metaphysical poets'?
A. They made an inappropriate combination of wit and imagination.
B. Instead of writing poetry, they only wrote verses.
C. They neither copied nature nor life.
D. They never tried to be singular in their thoughts.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In 'Life of Cowley' (from Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets, 1779), Samuel Johnson faults the metaphysical poets for merely writing verses rather than true poetry (B) and for neither copying nature nor human life (C).

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In "The Function of Criticism at the Present Time" what is proposed by Matthew Arnold as the essence of criticism?
items.explanation: In 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time' (1864), Matthew Arnold defines the essence of criticism as 'disinterestedness'—keeping aloof from partisan practical politics to 'see the object as in itself it really is.'

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · Andrew Marvell, T. S. Eliot
items.stem: How does T.S.Eliot sum up the peculiar quality of Marvell’s "Horatian Ode"?
options: 'a tough reasonableness beneath a slight lyric grace'
'a contrast of ideas, different in degree but the same in principle'
items.explanation: In his 1921 tercentenary essay 'Andrew Marvell', T.S. Eliot famously characterized Marvell's wit and the distinctive poetic quality of 'An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland' as 'a tough reasonableness beneath a slight lyric grace'.

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · F. R. Leavis
items.stem:
In his recasting the canon of English poetry in New Bearings in English Poetry which of the following pairs was
downgraded by F.R.Leavis ?
items.explanation: In New Bearings in English Poetry (1932), F.R. Leavis downgraded Victorian poets Alfred Tennyson and Algernon Charles Swinburne for escapist musicality while championing G.M. Hopkins, T.S. Eliot, and Ezra Pound.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Words with the same pronunciation and different meanings are:
items.explanation: In lexical semantics, 'homophones' (from Greek homo- 'same' and phone 'sound') are words that share identical pronunciation but differ in meaning and often spelling, such as 'two/too' or 'knight/night.'

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
According to Ferdinand de Saussure, language is:
A. an interlocking structure.
B. a system of constant change.
C. a system of signs.
D. a self-standing formation.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Course in General Linguistics (1916), Ferdinand de Saussure defines language (langue) synchronically as an interlocking relational structure (A) and a formal system of signs (C) wherein value is determined by differential relations.

items.title: Q18 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: The set of inflected forms taken by a single word is:
items.explanation: In morphology, a 'lexeme' is the abstract vocabulary unit underlying the entire set of inflected word-forms taken by a single word (such as give, gives, gave, given, and giving).

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which pair of linguists in the following list is associated with 'speech acts'?
items.explanation: Speech act theory was founded by Oxford philosopher J.L. Austin in How to Do Things with Words (1962) and systematically developed by his student John Searle in Speech Acts (1969).

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Usage in "You have hissed the mystery lectures." is an example of:
items.explanation: 'You have hissed the mystery lectures' (for 'You have missed the history lectures') is a classic 'spoonerism'—an accidental transposition of initial consonant sounds of two words, named after Oxford warden Reverend William Archibald Spooner.

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Ngugi wa Thiong'o
items.stem: Who wrote the short story, "The Voter"?
items.explanation: Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe wrote the satirical short story 'The Voter' (1965, collected in Girls at War and Other Stories, 1972), depicting electoral bribery through the character Rufus Okeke ('Roof').

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which character in Hamlet utters the line: "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark"?
items.explanation: In Act 1, Scene 4 of Shakespeare's Hamlet, the palace guard officer Marcellus speaks the famous line 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark' as Hamlet follows the Ghost on the battlements of Elsinore.

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Charles Lamb
items.stem: Who wrote the essay "My First Acquaintance with Poets"?
items.explanation: Romantic critic William Hazlitt wrote the autobiographical essay 'My First Acquaintance with Poets' (published in The Liberal in 1823), vividly recalling his youthful 1798 visit to Samuel Taylor Coleridge and William Wordsworth.

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Who wrote a postmodern reworking of Charles Dickens's Great Expectations without altering the original title?
items.explanation: American experimental punk-feminist writer Kathy Acker published her postmodern cut-up pastiche novel Great Expectations in 1982, appropriating Charles Dickens's exact title and opening lines.

items.title: Q25 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Anthony Burgess
items.stem: Who, in "The World as India," argues that English can be the only common "unifying language" of India?
items.explanation: American critic Susan Sontag delivered the 2002 St. Jerome Lecture on literary translation titled 'The World as India' (collected in At the Same Time, 2007), reflecting on English in multilingual India.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem: In which book of Paradise Lost does Milton refer to "Agra and Lahore of Great Mogul"?
items.explanation: In Book XI (line 391) of John Milton's Paradise Lost, the Archangel Michael leads Adam to the highest hill of Paradise and shows him a vision of future Asian empires, including 'Agra and Lahor of great Mogul.'

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Michel Foucault
items.stem: Which of the following narrative cycles is referred to in Michel Foucault' s "What is an Author?"?
items.explanation: In his 1969 lecture 'What Is an Author?,' Michel Foucault cites The Thousand and One Nights (Arabian Nights), where Scheherazade tells stories nightly to forestall execution, as an archetype of narrative warding off death.

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · G. K. Chesterton
items.stem: Who is the author of "The Typology of Detective Fiction"?
items.explanation: Bulgarian-French structuralist critic Tzvetan Todorov authored the 1966 essay 'The Typology of Detective Fiction' (collected in The Poetics of Prose, 1971), distinguishing the whodunit, the thriller, and the suspense novel.

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · George Herbert
items.stem:
Who among the following says that ideology is "a representation of the imaginary relationship of individuals to their real
conditions of existence"?
items.explanation: French Marxist philosopher Louis Althusser formulated the famous thesis that 'Ideology represents the imaginary relationship of individuals to their real conditions of existence' in 'Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses' (1970).

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope, Samuel Johnson, Thomas Gray, Horace
items.stem:
Which two among the following condemned the transportation of 50000 slaves into England in 1771?
A. Samuel Johnson
B. Alexander Pope
C. Horace Walpole
D. Thomas Gray
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Eighteenth-century writers Samuel Johnson (A)—who famously toasted 'to the next insurrection of the negroes in the West Indies'—and Horace Walpole (C) both condemned the British Atlantic slave trade in the 1770s.

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Ted Hughes
items.stem:
Which two are the works of Ted Hughes?
A. Wildtrack
B. Wodwo

C. Lupercal
D. Jack Straw's Castle
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Lupercal (1960, C) and Wodwo (1967, B) are major poetry collections by British Poet Laureate Ted Hughes, whereas Wildtrack (1965) was written by John Wain and Jack Straw's Castle (1976) by Thom Gunn.

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · I. A. Richards
items.stem:
Which two of the following are works by I. A. Richards?
A. Concepts of Criticism
B. Science and Poetry
C. The Philosophy of Rhetoric
D. English Literature in Our Time and the University
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: British critic I.A. Richards authored Science and Poetry (1926, B) and The Philosophy of Rhetoric (1936, C), whereas Concepts of Criticism is by René Wellek and English Literature in Our Time and the University is by F.R. Leavis.

items.title: Q33 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Which two of the following essays form part of Mikhail Bakhtin's The Dialogic Imagination: Four Essays?
A. "From the History of Novelistic Discourse"
B. "Discourse in the Novel"
C. "Romance and Novel"
D. "Forms of Time and the Chronotope in the Novel"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Mikhail Bakhtin's The Dialogic Imagination: Four Essays (edited by Michael Holquist, 1981) contains 'Epic and Novel,' 'From the Prehistory of Novelistic Discourse,' 'Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel' (D), and 'Discourse in the Novel' (B).

items.title: Q34 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Judith Wright
items.stem:
Which two of the following poems are by Judith Wright?
A. "Meditation on a Bone"
B. "Imperial Adam"
C. "Woman to Man"
D. "The Old Prison"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: 'Woman to Man' (1949, C) and 'The Old Prison' (D) are celebrated lyrics by Australian poet Judith Wright, whereas 'Meditation on a Bone' and 'Imperial Adam' were written by A.D. Hope.

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which two of the following are the earliest colonial publishing initiatives that apply to India?
A. Andrew Lang Colonial Book Series
B. Murray Colonial and Home Library Series

C. Colonial Library Series by Macmillan
D. Colonial Library Series by Chatto & Windus
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: John Murray's Colonial and Home Library (launched 1843, B) and Macmillan's Colonial Library (launched 1886, C) were the two pioneering British colonial book-publishing series targeting readers in colonial India.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jamaica Kincaid
items.stem:
Which two of the following conform to the documentation style prescribed by the eighth edition of the MLA Handbook?
A. Puig, Manuel. Kiss of the Spider Woman, translated by Thomas Colchie, Vintage Books, 1991.
B. Kincaid, Jamaica. "In History." Callaloo, vol. 24, no. 2, Spring 2001, pp. 620-26.
C. Nunberg, Geoffrey, editor. The Future of the Book. U of California P, 1996.
D. Wellek, Rene. A History of Modern Criticism, 1750-1950, Yale UP, 1986.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Entries B (Jamaica Kincaid's journal article) and C (Geoffrey Nunberg's edited volume) strictly follow the eighth edition of the MLA Handbook (2016) by placing a period after the title of the source before the container/contributor details.

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Matthew Arnold
items.stem:
Which two of the following are fallacious evaluations of poetry according to Matthew Arnold's "The Study of Poetry"?
A. contextual estimate
B. personal estimate
C. comparative estimate
D. historic estimate
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In 'The Study of Poetry' (1880), Matthew Arnold warns critics against two fallacious modes of judging poetry—the 'historic estimate' (D) and the 'personal estimate' (B)—which obscure the 'real estimate.'

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Derek Walcott, Wole Soyinka
items.stem:
Match List I with List II
List I
List II
Plays                                   Playwrights
A. Madmen and Specialists
I. Dennis Scott

B. The Sea at Dauphin
II. Wole Soyinka
C. The Trial of Dedan KimathiIII. Derek Walcott
D. An Echo in the Bone
IV. Ngugi wa Thiong'o
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Madmen and Specialists (1970) was written by Wole Soyinka (A-II), The Sea at Dauphin (1954) by Derek Walcott (B-III), The Trial of Dedan Kimathi (1976) by Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o and Micere Githae Mugo (C-IV), and An Echo in the Bone (1974) by Dennis Scott (D-I).

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following journals in the chronological order of publication.
 A. Longman's Magazine

 B. Cornhill Magazine
 C. Blackwood's Magazine
 D. Bentley's Miscellany
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: These nineteenth-century periodicals were founded in the chronological order: Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine (1817, C), Bentley's Miscellany (1836, D), The Cornhill Magazine (1860, B), and Longman's Magazine (1882, A).

items.title: Q40 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem:
Arrange the following poems by W. B. Yeats in the chronological order of publication.
 A. "The Wild Swans at Coole"
 B. "The Second Coming"
 C. "Among School Children"
 D. "Adam's Curse"
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of these poems by W.B. Yeats is 'Adam's Curse' (1902/1903, D), 'The Wild Swans at Coole' (1917, A), 'The Second Coming' (1920, B), and 'Among School Children' (1927, C).

items.title: Q41 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: The implied reader shifts attention from the real reading individual to a disembodied dimension of reception,
intricately interwoven into the text.
Reason R: The 'Dear Reader,' invoked in the realist novels, is a fictional representation of the distant reader.
In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: In Wolfgang Iser's reception theory (The Implied Reader, 1972), Assertion A accurately defines the implied reader as a textual structure of response, and Reason R is also true regarding the fictive 'Dear Reader' in realist novels, though R does not explain A.

items.title: Q42 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Samuel Beckett
items.stem:
Given below are two statements
Statement I: The opening and closing lines of Waiting for Godot are spoken by Estragon.
Statement II: Towards the end of the play Waiting for Godot, Estragon echoes Pozzo's statement, "They give birth astride
of a grave . . ."
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are false: in Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot, although Estragon speaks the opening line ('Nothing to be done'), Vladimir speaks the closing line ('Yes, let's go'), and it is Vladimir—not Estragon—who echoes Pozzo's 'Astride of a grave and a difficult birth.'

items.title: Q43 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Given below are two statements
Statement I: Language is not a reliable tool of communication, says deconstruction, but argues in favour of a theory of sign
as a self-sufficient union of signifier and signified.
Statement II: Deconstruction claims that language is non-referential since it refers neither to the things in the world nor to
our concepts of things but only to the play of signifiers.
In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
items.explanation: Statement I is incorrect because Jacques Derrida and deconstruction dismantle Saussure's stable union of signifier and signified; Statement II is correct because deconstruction views language as an endless differential play of signifiers (différance).

items.title: Q44 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which Shakespearean comedy is structured as a play within a play?
items.explanation: Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew opens with a framing 'Induction' in which a Lord tricks drunken tinker Christopher Sly into believing he is a nobleman watching a troupe of players perform the comedy of Petruchio and Katherina.

items.title: Q45 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following is a dead language?
items.explanation: Gothic is an extinct (dead) East Germanic language known primarily from fourth-century Bible translations by Bishop Ulfilas, whereas Frisian, Yiddish, and Cantonese are living languages.

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Mary Shelley
items.stem:
Which of the following fictional characters is believed to be based on the 15 -century real-life character, Vlad the
Impaler?
items.explanation: Irish author Bram Stoker named and loosely modeled the vampire antagonist Count Dracula in his 1897 Gothic novel Dracula after fifteenth-century Wallachian prince Vlad III ('Vlad the Impaler,' or Vlad Drăculea).

items.title: Q47 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following terms describes a novel of fashionable high life in 19 -century English literature?
items.explanation: 'Silver-fork' novels (a term coined by William Hazlitt in 1827) were a popular genre of 1820s–1840s British fiction—written by Catherine Gore, Edward Bulwer-Lytton, and Benjamin Disraeli—depicting the manners and etiquette of Regency high society.

items.title: Q48 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: What term did Bertolt Brecht use for his mode of drama-writing to distinguish it from traditional theatre?
items.explanation: German modernist playwright Bertolt Brecht championed 'epic theatre' (episches Theater), using episodic structure and the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) to provoke critical reflection rather than Aristotelian emotional catharsis.

items.title: Q49 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Who among the following posits the tradition of great writers as an inescapable fact, and takes the ambivalent
th
th

position of considering it as both a blessing and a curse?
items.explanation: In The Anxiety of Influence (1973), American critic Harold Bloom theorizes literary tradition as an inescapable Oedipal struggle in which strong precursor poets are simultaneously an enabling inspiration and an inhibiting curse for belated 'ephebes.'

items.title: Q50 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Who among the following is associated with a 'philosophy of praxis'?
items.explanation: Italian Marxist theorist Antonio Gramsci consistently referred to historical materialism and Marxism in his Prison Notebooks (1929–1935) as the 'philosophy of praxis,' emphasizing the unity of theoretical thought and revolutionary action.

items.title: Q51 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which book by J.G. Ballard is about a virus that freezes anything it comes in contact with?
items.explanation: British New Wave science-fiction writer J.G. Ballard's novel The Crystal World (1966) follows physician Edward Sanders into a Cameroonian jungle where a cosmic time-leakage phenomenon crystallizes plants, animals, and humans like a freezing virus.

items.title: Q52 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following terms is used to describe spurious words which are the result of inadvertent errors made
by copyists, printers and editors?
items.explanation: British philologist Walter William Skeat coined the term 'ghost-word' in 1886 to denote nonexistent, spurious words (such as 'abacot' or 'dord') that entered dictionaries solely through misprints or scribal errors.

items.title: Q53 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Frantz Fanon
items.stem: Which of the following statements best articulates Frantz Fanon's political position?
options: Colonialism will die a natural death sans any violent struggle against it
Social oppression in the third world is a matter more of race than of class
The African bourgeoisie can never succeed in the task of nation building
Peasants and social outcasts have little revolutionary potential in Africa
items.explanation: In 'The Pitfalls of National Consciousness' in The Wretched of the Earth (1961), Frantz Fanon argues that the post-independence African national bourgeoisie is an underdeveloped, neo-colonial intermediary incapable of genuine nation-building.

items.title: Q54 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Which of the following are books by Noam Chomsky?
A. Syntactic Structures
B. Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
C. Language and Society
D. Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
E. The Pragmatics of Politeness
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Syntactic Structures (1957, A) and Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965, D) are foundational linguistics monographs by Noam Chomsky, whereas The Pragmatics of Politeness (2014) was written by Geoffrey Leech.

items.title: Q55 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · James Joyce, Henry James, Charles Dickens, Henry Fielding
items.stem:
Which among the following are examples of the Künstlerroman?
A. The Portrait of a Lady
B. David Copperfield
C. Tom Jones
D. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: A Künstlerroman ('artist's novel') traces the formative development of a writer or artist from childhood to artistic maturity, exemplified by Charles Dickens's David Copperfield (1850, B) and James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916, D).

items.title: Q56 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following are novels by David Lodge?
A. The British Museum is Falling down
B. The Seven Sisters
C. Changing Places
D. Nice Work
E. Empire of the Sun
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: British novelist and critic David Lodge authored The British Museum Is Falling Down (1965, A), as well as the campus trilogy installments Changing Places (1975, C) and Nice Work (1988, D), whereas The Seven Sisters is by Margaret Drabble and Empire of the Sun by J.G. Ballard.

items.title: Q57 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are true of English as used in India?
A. India is counted among the largest English-speaking communities in the world.
B. No group, community or population of Indians claims English as its mother tongue.
C. More than fifty per cent of Indians speak English fluently.
D. English is the country's principal language of commerce.
E. With the growing stature of Hindi as lingua franca, it has supplanted English as the link language between the
central government and the states.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: India possesses one of the largest English-speaking populations globally (A) and uses English as its principal language of corporate and higher commerce (D), whereas statements B, C, and E are factually inaccurate.

items.title: Q58 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit I: Drama · William Wordsworth, Robert Browning, Alfred Tennyson, Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem:

List II

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Among nineteenth-century verse and stage dramas, Robert Browning wrote Strafford (1837, A-V), S.T. Coleridge wrote Remorse (1813, B-III), A.W. Pinero wrote The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893, C-II), Alfred Tennyson wrote Queen Mary (1875, D-I), and William Wordsworth wrote The Borderers (1796–97, E-IV).

items.title: Q59 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · George Herbert, Andrew Marvell, John Donne

B. The Temple
II. John Donne
C. The Rehearsal Transpros'dIII. George Herbert
D. Pindarique Odes
IV. Andrew Marvell
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Anniversaries (1611–12) were written by John Donne (A-II), The Temple (1633) by George Herbert (B-III), the prose satire The Rehearsal Transpros'd (1672–73) by Andrew Marvell (C-IV), and Pindarique Odes (1656) by Abraham Cowley (D-I).

items.title: Q60 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · D. H. Lawrence, E. M. Forster, Aldous Huxley, Graham Greene
items.stem:

items.explanation: A Handful of Dust (1934) was written by Evelyn Waugh (A-II), Brighton Rock (1938) by Graham Greene (B-V), Howards End (1910) by E.M. Forster (C-I), The Plumed Serpent (1926) by D.H. Lawrence (D-III), and Those Barren Leaves (1925) by Aldous Huxley (E-IV).

items.title: Q61 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange in the right sequence the following stages of a child's first language acquisition:
 A. holophrastic
 B. babbling

 C. telegraphic speech
 D. cooing
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In developmental psycholinguistics, a child's first-language acquisition progresses sequentially from cooing (D, ~2–5 months) to babbling (B, ~6–11 months), the holophrastic or one-word stage (A, ~12–18 months), and telegraphic speech (C, ~24–30 months).

items.title: Q62 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Shashi Deshpande, Arundhati Roy, Jhumpa Lahiri, Kiran Desai
items.stem:
Choose the right chronological sequence of the following books:
 A. Arundhati Roy, The God of Small Things
 B. Kiran Desai, The Inheritance of Loss
 C. Shashi Deshpande, That Long Silence
 D.  Jhumpa Lahiri, The Namesake
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: These Indian English novels were published in the chronological order: Shashi Deshpande's That Long Silence (1988, C), Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things (1997, A), Jhumpa Lahiri's The Namesake (2003, D), and Kiran Desai's The Inheritance of Loss (2006, B).

items.title: Q63 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following terms in the chronological order as these appeared in literary theory:
 A. phallogocentrism
 B. locutionary act
 C. interpellation
 D. interpretive community
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological order of these theoretical terms is J.L. Austin's 'locutionary act' (1955/1962, B), Louis Althusser's 'interpellation' (1970, C), Jacques Derrida's 'phallogocentrism' (1973–74, A), and Stanley Fish's 'interpretive community' (1976/1980, D).

items.title: Q64 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: All research being original and uninspired, it is rare for a researcher to begin a project by deriving ideas
from predecessors.
Statement II: Studying and documenting past work on a research topic stifles the continual expansion of human
knowledge.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
items.explanation: Both statements are incorrect: scholarly research always builds upon a thorough literature review of prior scholarship, and documenting earlier work is essential to advancing rather than stifling human knowledge.

items.title: Q65 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: A pidgin is formed by two mutually unintelligible speech communities trying to communicate using the
most obvious features of each other's language.
Statement II: Notwithstanding the number of years a pidgin is spoken, it can never become the mother tongue of a
community.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
items.explanation: A pidgin arises as a simplified contact language between speech communities lacking a common tongue (Statement I is correct); however, when a pidgin is acquired by children as their native mother tongue, it develops into a creole (Statement II is incorrect).

items.title: Q66 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Dekker, John Marston, Ben Jonson, Thomas Middleton
items.stem:
Which of the following are true of the dramatic legacy of Ben Jonson?
A. Jonson's physiological interpretation of character and personality did not have any precedent.
B. Taking after the practice of the Moralities and Interludes, Jonson named his dramatis personae aptronymically.
C. Chapman's All Fools and Middleton's A Trick to Catch the Old One belong to the genre of Comedy of Humours that
Jonson is said to have pioneered.
D. John Marston and Thomas Dekker collaborated with Jonson in writing for a children's company of players.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Ben Jonson followed medieval morality plays in giving characters aptronymic names reflecting their dominant traits (B), and George Chapman's All Fools and Thomas Middleton's A Trick to Catch the Old One share the Jonsonian Comedy of Humours / city-comedy tradition (C).

items.title: Q67 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who is the author of The Truth about Me: A Hijra Life Story?
items.explanation: Transgender rights activist and writer A. Revathi authored the landmark autobiography The Truth About Me: A Hijra Life Story (2010), translated from Tamil into English by feminist historian V. Geetha.

items.title: Q68 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Gabriel Garcia Marquez
items.stem: Who wrote The Labyrinth of Solitude?
items.explanation: Mexican poet, diplomat, and 1990 Nobel laureate Octavio Paz wrote The Labyrinth of Solitude (El laberinto de la soledad, 1950), a classic collection of essays analyzing Mexican national identity and history.

items.title: Q69 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: What was the centre set up for studying culture at the University of Birmingham called?
items.explanation: Founded by Richard Hoggart in 1964 at the University of Birmingham and later directed by Stuart Hall, the pioneering research institute was named the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS).

items.title: Q70 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Gustave Flaubert
items.stem: Who is the creator of the character, Julien Sorel?
items.explanation: French realist novelist Stendhal (Marie-Henri Beyle) created the ambitious provincial young protagonist Julien Sorel in his masterpiece The Red and the Black (Le Rouge et le Noir, 1830).

items.title: Q71 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Which of these are true of Raymond Williams' Culture and Society?
A. It critiques the idea of high culture.
B. It overlooks the idea of high culture.
C. It defines culture as a way of life.
D. It equates culture with science.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Culture and Society: 1780–1950 (1958), Raymond Williams critiques elitist bourgeois notions of 'high' minority culture (A) and argues democratically that culture is 'a whole way of life' (C).

items.title: Q72 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Which of the following does Urvashi Butalia's The Other Side of Silence primarily seek to do?
A. To understand the Partition as something more than a political divide
B. To foreground a personal history of the Partition
C. To foreground the Partition as an event more tragic than the Holocaust
D. To find and unite families separated at the Partition
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Urvashi Butalia's oral history The Other Side of Silence: Voices from the Partition of India (1998) moves beyond high-political constitutional history (A) to recover the silenced personal testimonies of women, children, and marginalized survivors (B).

items.title: Q73 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Upamanyu Chatterjee, Rohinton Mistry, Anita Desai

items.explanation: English, August (1988) was written by Upamanyu Chatterjee (A-IV), In Custody (1984) by Anita Desai (B-II), Such a Long Journey (1991) by Rohinton Mistry (C-III), and Funny Boy (1994) by Shyam Selvadurai (D-I).

items.title: Q74 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Which of these may be said to be true of the journal published from Bowling Green University from 1969, which
carried essays on Spiderman comics, rock music, and detective films?
A. It sought to highlight the importance of popular culture.
B. It sought to highlight the importance of elite culture.
C. It sought to buttress the canon by making it more elitist.
D. It sought to break down the dominance of 'high' culture.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Journal of Popular Culture, published at Bowling Green State University, legitimized the academic study of everyday mass culture (A) and challenged the canonical monopoly of elite 'high' culture (D).

items.title: Q75 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roland Barthes, Homi K. Bhabha

items.explanation: Homi K. Bhabha authored The Location of Culture (1994, A-II), T.S. Eliot wrote Notes towards the Definition of Culture (1948, B-III), Roland Barthes's essays were collected in Image-Music-Text (1977, C-IV), and John Fiske wrote Reading the Popular (1989, D-I).

items.title: Q76 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit II: Poetry · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem:
Who, among these, are songwriters who have been awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature?
A. Elton John
B. Rabindranath Tagore
C. Bob Dylan
D. Bob Marley

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Bengali polymath Rabindranath Tagore (who composed over two thousand Rabindra Sangeet songs and won the 1913 Nobel Prize, B) and American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan (awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize, C) are both Nobel Literature laureates.

items.title: Q77 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following qualify for the label 'cultural intermediary' in the context of a commercial film?
A. The film magazine columnist
B. The director
C. Fan clubs
D. The producer
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Pierre Bourdieu's sociology of culture, film magazine columnists (A) and organized fan clubs (C) act as 'cultural intermediaries' who mediate reception and shape taste between primary film producers (the director and producer) and the public.

items.title: Q78 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following is true of mass media?
options: It usually has a central, single source
Its audience is in close proximity to its source
It can affect a localised population only
items.explanation: In communication theory, traditional mass media (such as broadcast television, radio, and print newspapers) is characterized by one-to-many transmission from a single, centralized institutional source to a large, dispersed audience.

items.title: Q79 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
With which of the following movements is Charles Baudelaire's Flowers of Evil generally associated?
A. Neo-classical
B. Symbolist
C. Modernist
D. Postmodernist
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Charles Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du mal (The Flowers of Evil, 1857) is a foundational precursor of the French Symbolist movement (B) and inaugurated lyric Modernism (C) through its urban flâneur sensibility.

items.title: Q80 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Which of these departments did the Wood's Despatch of 1854 recommend setting up in the universities?
A. Arabic

B. English
C. French
D. Law
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Paragraph 30 of Sir Charles Wood's Despatch of 1854 recommended establishing university professorships in Law (D), Civil Engineering, English (B), and classical Oriental languages including Arabic (A), Sanskrit, and Persian.

items.title: Q81 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Which of these are generally taken to be true of Cultural Studies?
A. It is politically engaged.
B. It privileges text over context.
C. It has a symbiotic relationship with Formalism.
D. It studies the means of production of a text.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Cultural Studies is an explicitly politically engaged discipline examining power, ideology, and hegemony (A), and it investigates the material and institutional means of cultural production and reception (D) rather than privileging isolated formalist texts.

items.title: Q82 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Michel de Montaigne
items.stem: Which of these countries does Montaigne’s essay, "Of Cannibals," focus on primarily?
items.explanation: In 'Of Cannibals' (1580), Michel de Montaigne describes the indigenous Tupinambá people of Brazil (part of France's brief colony France Antarctique), using their lifestyle to critique the corruption, violence, and hypocrisy of 16th-century European civilization.

items.title: Q83 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Ruskin Bond
items.stem:
Arrange the following characters in the chronological order in which they appeared in Indian literature.
 A. Praneshacharya (Samskara)
 B. Sakuni (Mahabharata)
 C. Rusty (The Room on the Roof)
 D. Gobar (Godan)
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: These characters appeared in Indian literature in the chronological order: Shakuni in Vyasa's ancient Sanskrit epic Mahabharata (B), Gobar in Munshi Premchand's Hindi novel Godaan (1936, D), Rusty in Ruskin Bond's The Room on the Roof (1956, C), and Praneshacharya in U.R. Ananthamurthy's Kannada novel Samskara (1965, A).

items.title: Q84 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit I: Drama · Vijay Tendulkar
items.stem: Which of these themes best sums up the preoccupation of most of Vijay Tendulkar's plays?
items.explanation: Marathi playwright Vijay Tendulkar's major plays—including Silence! The Court Is in Session (1967), Sakharam Binder (1972), and Ghashiram Kotwal (1972)—centrally interrogate the brutal workings of political, patriarchal, and institutional power.

items.title: Q85 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of these is identified by Ariel Dorfman and Armand Mattelart as having been deployed in Walt Disney comicbooks
to propagate imperialist ideology?
items.explanation: In How to Read Donald Duck (1971), Ariel Dorfman and Armand Mattelart demonstrate how Walt Disney comics deploy 'infantilisation'—portraying Third World colonized peoples as naive children—to naturalize American imperialist domination.

items.title: Q87 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Which of the following did Owuor Anyumba, Taban Lo Liyong and Ngugi wa Thiongo object to in 1968?
A. the primacy of English literatures and cultures
B. the centrality of Africa in the Department of English
C. the primacy of orature in the syllabus
D. the focus on the study of the historic continuity of English literature
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In their landmark 1968 University of Nairobi memorandum 'On the Abolition of the English Department,' Henry Owuor-Anyumba, Taban Lo Liyong, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o objected to the colonial primacy of English literature (A) and the assumption of its historic continuity as the center of study (D).

items.title: Q88 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser, William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem:
Arrange chronologically the following texts in terms of their years of first publication:
 A. Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene
 B. Coleridge and Wordsworth's Lyrical Ballads
 C. Pablo Neruda's Canto General
 D. Charles Baudelaire's The Flowers of Evil
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of first publication is Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1590, A), Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads (1798, B), Charles Baudelaire's The Flowers of Evil (1857, D), and Pablo Neruda's Canto General (1950, C).

items.title: Q89 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Samuel Beckett
items.stem:
Which of these characters figure in Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot?
A. Estragon
B. Pozzo
C. Bassanio
D. Murphy
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Estragon ('Gogo,' A) and Pozzo (B) are major characters in Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953), whereas Bassanio appears in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice and Murphy is the title protagonist of Beckett's 1938 novel.

items.title: Q90 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Probal Dasgupta
items.stem: Who is the author of The Otherness of English: India’s Aunty Tongue Syndrome?
items.explanation: Linguist Probal Dasgupta authored 'The Otherness of English: India's Auntie Tongue Syndrome' (1993), analyzing the sociolinguistic tension in India where English functions as an 'auntie tongue'—an external language of mobility and authority—alongside indigenous mother tongues.

items.title: Q91 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)

items.explanation: Connemara Public Library (established 1896) is in Chennai (A-II), C.D. Narasimhaiah's literary center Dhvanyaloka is in Mysore (B-III), the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute is in Pune (C-IV), and the Asiatic Society (1784) is in Kolkata (D-I).

items.title: Q92 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Arrange the following groups of poets in their chronological sequence in relation to English literary history:
 A. The Imagist poets
 B. The Cavalier poets
 C. The Movement poets
 D. The Lake poets
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: These poetic schools appeared in English literary history in the sequence: the Cavalier poets (1630s–1640s, B), the Romantic Lake poets (1790s–1830s, D), the Modernist Imagist poets (1912–1917, A), and the postwar Movement poets (1950s, C).

items.title: Q94 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following terms in their chronological sequence of appearance:
 A. dissociation of sensibility
 B. unreliable narrator
 C. theatre of cruelty
 D. egotistical sublime
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of these critical terms is John Keats's 'egotistical sublime' (1818, D), T.S. Eliot's 'dissociation of sensibility' (1921, A), Antonin Artaud's 'Theatre of Cruelty' (1932–38, C), and Wayne C. Booth's 'unreliable narrator' (1961, B).

items.title: Q96 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which of the following abbreviations refers to a documentation style?
items.explanation: MHRA stands for the Modern Humanities Research Association, which publishes the widely used MHRA Style Guide for academic documentation, whereas PMLA, ARIEL, and MFS are literary journals.

items.title: Q97 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: The MLA Style Sheet, a compilation of scholarly conventions and directives, was first published in:
items.explanation: The Modern Language Association (MLA) first published 'The MLA Style Sheet' in 1951 (compiled by William Riley Parker), establishing standardized citation guidelines for academic research in literature and modern languages.

items.title: Q98 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Who among the following has coined the term, 'ecofeminism'?
items.explanation: French feminist writer Françoise d'Eaubonne coined the term 'ecofeminism' (l'écoféminisme) in her 1974 book Le Féminisme ou la Mort (Feminism or Death), linking patriarchal domination of women with ecological exploitation.

items.title: Q99 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Late Antiquity & Patristic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Jerome
items.stem: Who is the author of Radiant Textuality?
items.explanation: American textual scholar Jerome McGann authored Radiant Textuality: Literature after the World Wide Web (2001), exploring digital humanities, hypertext archives, and editorial theory.

items.title: Q100 · Dec 2021 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Arrange the following in their chronological order:
 A. English replaces Persian as official language of the Company
 B. Arrival of Charles Grant in India
 C. Universities established in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras
 D. Construction of Fort William in Calcutta
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological sequence of these events in British India is the construction of Fort William in Calcutta (1696–1700, D), the arrival of East India Company official Charles Grant in India (1767, B), English replacing Persian as official language (1835/1837, A), and the founding of the Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras (1857, C).
